newsitem.title: KENYA: Go-slow by Kenya air traffic controllers ends.
newsitem.headline: Go-slow by Kenya air traffic controllers ends.

text.p: A go-slow by Kenyan air traffic controllers ended on Thursday with agreement with the government and flights returned to normal after five days of cancellations and delays.
"The situation is back to normal. We have explained what the government is trying to do and they (controllers) have understood and cooperated," Labour Minister Philip Masinde told a news conference.
He declined to give any details of the agreement to end the go-slow, which had entered a sixth day earlier on Thursday.

But air controllers told Reuters they returned to normal work after being assured that a report presented to President Daniel arap Moi on Wednesday on the terms and conditions of service for government workers would meet their concerns.

"We are back to work as normal. People are very selfish so we decided to go back. We are waiting to see if they deliver on promises in two weeks' time. We don't know what they are planning to give us. There are no delays now," a controller at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International airport told Reuters.
Air traffic controllers had demanded a 50-fold increase in what they say is pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
On Tuesday, Masinde had ordered the controllers to open negotiations and resume work but the order was ignored.

The go-slow was resolved after foreign airlines and freight forwarders said they were increasingly concerned about safety at Nairobi's airport with flights circling the Kenyan capital for hours waiting to land.

At least 40 airlines use Kenyan airports and landing and parking fees brings millions of dollars in revenue. The go-slow forced many airlines to cancel flights while others were delayed for up to 12 hours.
Airports at Nairobi, the coast city of Mombasa, Kisumu and the tourist resort of Malindi were hit hard by the dispute.

The go-slow had increased pressure on a government hit by the International Monetary Fund's decision last week to halt a $205 million aid package, citing concern at corruption, and facing a Friday general strike called by an opposition-backed alliance.
